notes.meaning: After surviving the violent storm and shipwreck, the travelers learned that the island was Malta, located south of Sicily. God kept His promise to protect everyone on board, bringing all two hundred and seventy-six passengers safely ashore.

The islanders showed remarkable warmth and hospitality to the wet and shivering survivors. Ancient writers called these people barbarians simply because they spoke Phoenician instead of Greek or Latin, not because they were uncivilized. They immediately built a large fire to give everyone relief from the rain and bitter cold.

Even though Paul was an apostle and an elderly prisoner, he gladly served others by gathering a bundle of firewood. A poisonous snake had been sleeping in the twigs to escape the winter chill, and the heat woke it up. As Paul placed the sticks on the fire, the viper fastened its fangs onto his hand.

When the local people saw the snake dangling from Paul's hand and noticed he was a prisoner, they jumped to the conclusion that he was a murderer. They believed in a goddess of justice who punished evil deeds. They assumed that even though he escaped the raging sea, divine vengeance had caught up with him.

Paul calmly shook the snake into the flames without panicking. The venom did not harm him at all. God kept His servant completely safe so that Paul could fulfill his calling to preach the gospel in Rome.

The islanders watched closely, expecting Paul's body to swell with terrible inflammation or drop dead on the spot. After waiting a long time with nothing going wrong, they completely changed their minds. In their superstition, they decided that Paul must be a god rather than a criminal.

The leading Roman official on the island, a man named Publius, owned an estate in that area. He welcomed Paul and his traveling companions with great courtesy. He generously provided lodging and food for them during their first three days on the island.

Publius's father was bedridden with recurring fevers and severe dysentery. Paul went in to see the sick man, prayed to show that God is the true healer, and laid his hands on him. God answered the prayer immediately and healed the man.
Word of this miraculous cure quickly spread across the island. Soon, people brought everyone who was sick or disabled to Paul. God demonstrated His great mercy and power by healing all who came.

The islanders showed deep appreciation to Paul and his companions through many expressions of honor and respect. When spring arrived and it was time to set sail, the people generously supplied them with all the food and provisions needed for the voyage.

After spending three winter months on Malta, the group set sail on another grain ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter in a nearby harbor. The vessel carried a carved figurehead of the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux. Ancient pagan sailors looked to these mythical figures for protection at sea.

The ship sailed about eighty miles north to Syracuse, the famous capital city of Sicily. The crew anchored there for three days, likely waiting for favorable winds before attempting the next leg of the journey.

From Syracuse, the ship tacked along the coast to Rhegium on the southern tip of the Italian mainland. A favorable south wind sprang up the following day, allowing them to sail quickly up the coast to Puteoli, a major Roman port near Naples.

Upon landing at Puteoli, Paul was overjoyed to find local Christian believers who invited him and his friends to stay for a full week. The Roman centurion kindly allowed this delay, showing continued respect for Paul. After this refreshing visit, they set out by land toward Rome.

Believers from Rome heard that Paul was approaching and walked more than forty miles down the Appian Way to meet him at the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns. Meeting these loving brothers and sisters deeply cheered Paul. Their presence encouraged his heart and moved him to give thanks to God.

When they reached Rome, the Roman authorities granted Paul special consideration because he was not considered dangerous. Instead of being locked away in a harsh public prison, he was permitted to live in private lodgings. A single Roman soldier remained with him to guard him.

After three days of rest, Paul invited the local Jewish leaders to his lodging. Because he was under guard and could not visit their synagogues, he brought them together to explain his situation. He assured them that he had done nothing against the Jewish people or their ancestral customs.

Paul told the leaders that Roman governors in Judea had examined him thoroughly. After hearing the accusations, the Romans found no evidence of any crime deserving the death penalty. They had wanted to release him on the spot.

Paul explained that when certain religious leaders in Judea opposed his release, he had no choice but to appeal his case to Caesar to preserve his life. He made it clear that he took this step strictly for self-defense. He was not there to bring charges or air grievances against his own nation.

Paul explained that he had called them together so they could hear the truth directly from him. He pointed out the chain around his wrist and explained that he wore it because of the hope of Israel. He was a prisoner for believing in the promised Messiah and the resurrection of the dead.

The Jewish leaders replied that they had not received any official letters about Paul from Judea, nor had any travelers brought bad reports about him. God shielded Paul from their plots, likely because his accusers realized they could not win their case before the emperor and let the matter drop.

The leaders said they wanted to hear Paul present his own teachings and arguments. They knew that the Christian movement was criticized and opposed everywhere, but they were still willing to give Paul a fair, firsthand hearing.

They set a specific day, and a large crowd came to Paul’s lodging to listen. From morning until evening, Paul patiently explained the spiritual nature of God’s kingdom. He walked them through the Law of Moses and the Prophets, proving from the Old Testament Scriptures that Jesus is the promised Messiah.

Paul’s long teaching brought a divided response, which is common whenever the gospel is preached. Some of the hearers were persuaded by the biblical evidence and believed in Jesus. Others hardened their hearts and refused to accept the message.

The meeting broke up amid sharp disagreement between those who believed and those who did not. As the guests began to walk out, Paul gave one last solemn warning. He declared that the Holy Spirit had spoken accurately through the prophet Isaiah when describing their ancestors.

Paul quoted Isaiah to explain why so many people reject God's truth. The prophet had warned that people would hear the words without understanding and look without really seeing. Their hearts had grown dull and stubborn, choosing to close their eyes and stop their ears so they would not turn to God and receive His spiritual healing.

Because many of his Jewish listeners refused the good news, Paul declared that God's salvation was being sent directly to the Gentiles. He expressed full confidence that the non-Jewish nations would listen and welcome the gospel. God's saving grace would not be stopped by human unbelief.
After hearing Paul’s strong words from Scripture, the visitors departed and continued arguing among themselves. Those who had come to faith debated with those who still rejected Jesus.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars and translations note that this verse is absent from the oldest and most reliable Greek manuscripts, suggesting it was added by later copyists to smooth the transition.

notes.meaning: Paul stayed in Rome for two full years in his own rented lodging, paying his expenses while waiting for his case to be heard. He remained under guard, but he made the most of his time by warmly receiving everyone who came to see him.

Throughout those two years, Paul boldly preached God's kingdom and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ without anyone stopping him. Even though the apostle was bound in chains, the message of the gospel remained entirely free and unhindered. This open ending reminds the church that the mission of spreading the Good News continues.
